Kane ka kitab ka kyntbup ha ka ia ki phang bapher ba la thoh da ki nongthoh baphei kiba iadei bad ka Culture, History, Literature bad kiwei. Kura ban shu pynkynmaw, ka kitab ''Na Ka Thiar Ki Longshuwa” kaba lapynraih ha ka snera 1981 ka kynthup tang ia ki poitri Khasi kiba rira, hynrei ha kane ka kpti la pynrung ha kane ka kitab iaki jingthoh kiba iadei beit tang bad ka “Prose” Kane ka kitab ka don 14 tylli ki lynnong, kaba n}rngkong na Ki Poitri Khasi u Soso Thara, bad ia ki jingthoh kiba sah lasot na ka kot-khubor “Ka Syngkhong Jingtip’’. Khnang ban pynsuk ia ki samla shongskul hadlen habud la pyni ha “ki sher'* ia ki thymmei (Source) na kiba la shim ia kine ki jingthoh. Ngi kyrmen skhem ba ki symboh jingtip ha kane ka kitab kin long ka jingiarap ia kito ki riew-wad-jingtip kiba pule ia ka khamtam eh ki samla shongskul ha ki jingpule ki jong ki. Dated Shiltong) 18th May, 1984) Maurice G. Lyogdob Editor, Khasi Authors' Society KA JINGAIKHMAT da u Edrenel Chyne Ban pynpaw ia ka jingshisba bad ka jingitynnad kom ki mationg na kiei kiei ktba don ba ka marian^ habar bad faapoh fong ngi, ba ka dohnud u briew ka lah ban bat ban long ka jingshai ia' ka, ka long ka kam ka poetry. Ban thoh poetry ka donkam bail aon ka sap kaba pher. Naior bun kiei kiei ruh ka shong ha kaba thain ia -ka sur ki ktien, khnang ban pynpaw kyndiang ia ka jingitynnad ka jingmut; ka laid na ka shkor bad ka rung sha ka dohnud. Kumta haba pule ia ki poetry kiba bha ka at Jioghun bad jingtngen ia ka mynsiem kaba ngim ioh na kiwei pat ki jingpjte. Dei tang kiei kiei kiba mih na ka dohnud ktba lah ban rung shata. Ban thoh poetry ha ka ktien Khasi ka dei ban long kaba eh shibun namar (i) ka ktien hi ka long kaba khim eh, (ii) yin don lypa ki model, (iii) ka donkam ia u nongthoh ban da seng hi ia ki ain ka Khasi prosody.

Hynrei khamtam namar ka dohnud kari ka dang ryngkhiang eh. Naior Ki Phawer u Aesop, kiba don la ka jingsammut bad ka dur, u Mr. Soso 1 ham mynta u la pynmih pat sa ki verse ; hynrei um pat shon lut ia ki hangne. U la pynlut da ki snem ha kaba iatalon bad ki Titan jong kij'ingeh baroh : bad u la Ich kumba ong uwei u nongthoh, • "The poet devotes himself heart and soul to the work ; he alters this and that once, and again ; he sees fresh aspect of the thing and alters all again ; he writes and rewrites, getting deeper and deeper into the essential values of the thing all the time." Ha kane ka rukom u la iathain iapra ia ki bun wat. La kidd ki verse; ki la poi ne em ha ki rmiang bad ka synigiew ka poetry, ki nongpule bad ka por kin latai hi. Hynrei la ki lodg' kumno kumao run nga dei ban ong ba la thoh la ki ha loi ktieiV Khasi kaba paka tarn ha kane ka aiom. Don bun ki jin^iglHI' hangne ba ki briew ki dei ban nang. Ka jingthrou |i imnguiob ka long khamtam eh na ka bynta ki khynnah, ban ring ta ki sha kh jingitynnad ka mariang ha ia ka ktien bad ha la ka ri, iBa la shon ha Ki Poetry Kkapi (I995)>>274.2S jong m Thamj SHANO U SAJAR U LEIT ? Baroh'shi katta la bun tang ka ktien shii ong, bad ka pyrkhat khlem kam, hynrei mynta la sdang sa ka pyr&hang pynlong, bad hamar kane ka lap sa ka sngew del kioi Ian, hynrei shisha ban sngap ia kito kiba la jiw mlien ia ka kam, ki stfeng ba haba ka jia jyllei eh ka por lap syrwet syriem bad ka rai kloi Ian “ba hei kane la dei shane, bad thik dei kane” bunsicn poi sha khlaw. Shano U Sajar Myntri u leit ? Shaphang kane, shisien u trai shnong ka Ri Kbadar Lyngdoh Nongpoh u ong sngap ngan iathuh* khana sa ma^nga. MynbauSyiem Synteng u pan khyllung uwei uwei shi miet ban buh .pymyaid ha ki kjat jong u Syiem haba u thiah mynmiet, la win jlang u khun u raiot. fiuk ieng U Sajac Myntri bad ki bun spah kur na ri Synteng, sepngi ki iaid haduh ban da poi ha ka wah bah Umiam. Ym tip shuh kumno yn leh. Mynmiet mih u 'sbinbab u dem knep lyngknep na shiliang ha shiliang ka wah ba ta shlei, bad kdain ka long ka lynti bah.

laid u paid U Sajar sha shiliang. bad nangta long ki paid Khadar Lyngdoh jong ka Hima Nongpoh. Katto katne na uta u paid ki kiew artet .sha lum, u paid ba sah u saphnang sha sepngi. U Sajar rangbah shi'pai u tip la ka sain pyrthei, um iaid beit, um khwan ban kwah ia ka trh paid ha lade. Dei ban don da ki Siam ryngkat. Kumta pyrkhat uta u 'rirwpyrkhat bad u la lam ryngkat bad ki siem kynthei na ki Siem Syntene, u kit wallam ryngkot ryngkat sha Nongpoh, bad nangta ii iaid sha ki thain sepngi. Ki Nongpoh k> iathuh ba la ka dula (duli) jong U Sajar ba u bah ia ki Siem Kynthei, bad ka wait kaba wah ha ka dieng, bad u kynjri nar, ki don ha kawei ka khlaw, bad ia kita ki la pyni ha uwei u Sahep. Ban ym da bun ktien. kme ki jaid ki poi sha ri dkbar ha ki pud ka ri Gauhati bad ki shong shato, nangta ki kiew artet pat, ki sdang sha ki thaih Mawdem bad ha ki shnong bad ki it bad ia sin ia kita ki shnong, Ka It ka Hima Ri Khadsawphra. Kumta ki Siem lieh Khadsawphra ki la sngew ba ki ia dei kur bad ki Siem Synteng bad ngi shem ia ki Khadar Lyngdoh Ri Nongpoh. bad ki Jirang Ri Mynnar ba ki ia kem ha ka ktien bad ha ka jingmut bad ki Pngr, Kaei kaba ngi shem pat. Ki shala ki wan shong ha ' Pomshala na pdeng kita ki paid ba kiew artet. Ki riewtymmen dei U Khang, U Sahei» U Rhrang bad tl Ben, ki nongseng ia ki Mustoh bad Shala. Kioe ki Shala ki phet na Pomshala ka jaka happh lum Mawpat lam sepngi hajan Shillong, ^ ka jaka kaba ha neng law lyngdoh' Myllimn, bad nangta ki biar shathie. Kawei ar na ki sakhi ka pyni dak ba ki Pnar in kiba ngi sin ki Synteng, ki long ki jub ki briew bad fci Khadar Lyngdoh Nongpoh l»d ki briew ha ki thain Sepngi ka Ri Jirang Mynnar bad Khad- sawphra, bad kito kl jbriew shathie sha Shala, Mustph, Nongwar, ka Ktien.

Kane bad kiwei ki sakhi ka long ba u Khasi bad u Pnar u loAg tang uwei u ja,d bynriew, iada jtar na ka ktien ne ha kn kam kut kam kha, ne ha ka jingmut la U Blei bad la ka im ka iap; bad ka lynti laid ka long kaba shat ba une u jaid bynnew u tur na Mihngi sha Sepngi. la ka thymmei bad ka sdang, bad nangno ba wan u Khasi n Pnar, dei naneta haba sdang, la hyndai hynthai u Khasi la ka sngi u Khyndai na jrong bad u Hyn&ie# na ibian bid ter ter la ka shitom ka shijot haduh ba un da mgi shitom bad sah sa kamynsiem Kane pyribaii kumba nga la thoh ha kane ka byngkhong Jingtip ka long ka ktien jingstad, ka ticn sneng tien kraw, ban sah pateng kum ka jingkyniip la uba lah ka pyrkhat. Ha ka pyr'hei don ar jaid ki brirw. Don kiba ngeit la lade ba ki mih na kpoh ka khyndew na Ramia,^ don kiwei pat kiba ngeit ba ki hiar lane ba ki nongsynshar jong ki (a kumno-kumno ki hiar na Jrong, IJ Khasi pat u ong u Khyndai na jrong bad u Hynniew na tbian Hangno b^ kumno une (i Khasi u leit ong kumne.

Ka jingwad ban bud la ki sangara ki sajah bad ka jinghikai bad rukom pyrkhat bastad jong ka jingtip, kt lalam ia ngi sha ki bun kiei kidi» Phin map na ka bynta ka por bad ka jaka, bad phim kwahld lehse ba ogan ong bua ktien eh. David Roy IMS KA LITERATURE — Owen Rowie ' Kad kane kaba ki ong ka Literature ? I Uwei u nongthoh uba la bud bad wad bniah ia ki jingthoh bad ' ki jingtrei jong kiwei pat ki nongiboh bad nongrwai u la pyrshang batai.ia kane ka ktien da kumne. Ha kaba mynhyndai eh, ha kaba ym pat don ei ei satia ka jingtip shaphang ka jingthoh ne jingrwai, uwei u khynnah u ia tem kawei ka pnar narud duriaw; haba u ia ialehkai u ia kum bat ia ka hajan ka shkor bad u la kyndit ban tohsngew hapoh kata ka pnar ia ki jingsawa bad ki sur kiba sngewtynnad sliibun. Da kaba ryngkhat kumta uta u khyn* nah u la iohsngew ia ka jingrwai bathiang Jong ka tnanang baroh sawdong jong u, shaior bad shapoh. sha kadiang bad sha kamon. Ka Literature ka sriem ia katei ka pnar— ka long kum ka jing* tem kaba la pynbeit bha ia ki ksai ba ka jingim jong u briew bad ka mariang kan phalang na ka hala ki sur-ki sur kiba ia pynia- biang kat ban pynthiang ia ki kum ka jingrwai bad jingkyniid kaba sngewtynnad bad sngewbang, kaba shoh bad kyntiew la ka mynsiem jong ki briew shabar jong ki marwei-marwei ban phriang iaiade halor ki lum bad ki madan jong ka jinglong bad jingim briew ha ka mariang kaba u briew u don Ha kane ka rukom ka long kawei na kita ki jingstad kiba iapher (Artsj jong u briew kiba pynlong ia ka jingim jong u kaba myntoi bad kaba iaikynjnh sha> phrang ha ka jingsngew<huh bad ka jingroi ka jingmanbha. Ka long kata ka bynta jong ka jingstad kaba paw ha ki kot ki sla, ki kitab bad ki jingthoh kiba la-pateng-la-pateng naduh mynha u briew u dang sdang ban nang ban pynneh ha ki jingthoh-jingtar ia ki jingshem jong u haba u iaid lyngba ia ka jingim jong u ha kane Im pyrthei. Kita kiwei pat ki jaid jingstad da kiba u briew u pynsah pateng la ia ki jingshem bad ki jingsngew ki long ka Painting (Kajingthaw bad thoh dur), ka Sculpture (Ka jingo! ne sain dur), ka Architecture (Ka jingtei ia ki jingtei) bad ka Music (Ka Jingthaw sur jingrwai ne jingkynud). Haba shu kren kylluid, ngmarkata, ka Literature ka mut kl kot-ki-sla bad ki kitab ba la thoh bad ia thaw naduh mynhyndai haduh mynta bad ki jingthoh kiba ia thoh h^ kita ki kot-ki-sla bad ki kitab. Ha kane ka jingmut ngi kynthl^ ia ki jingthoh baroh kiba don ha ka pyrthei shaphang kawei-pa-kawei ka jingwad jingstad jong u briew, lada ka long shaphang ka bneng bad ki khlur kiba don ha ka (Astronomy); ne shaphang ki jitigiadei jong ki kynja met kawei bad kawei pat bad ki ain kiba synshar bad pyniaid ia ki (Physical Sciences); ne shaphang ka jinglong jong u briew ha ka pyrkhat-pyrdaifi bad ka jiogiadei jong ki mynsiem jong u bad kiei kiei kioa iakynduh bad o (Mental and Moral Sdences); pewat shaphang kitei ki sawtylli ki jaid jingstad kiba ia niew fcyrteng bapeng rah kiba ba kajuh-ka kyrdan jin^ong. jingtrei t»d ■^5 jingthmu kum ma ka hi-ka Painting, Sculpture, Architecture bad Music; bad ym tang katta hynrei wat shaphang ia lade hi ruh kunl ka Literature, la kine ki kot bad ki kitab kiba la thoh shaphang kine ki jingstad kiba iapher, natnarkata, ngi khot ia ki kawei pa kawei, ka Literature ha la kata ka bynta shaphang jong kaba kren lada ka long ka Astronomy, ka Painting ne kano fcatk<9- ka bynta jong ka jingwad* jingstad jong u briew. Kumta ha kane ka jingmut kaba kylluid kumne kane ka ktien "Literature” ka kynthup la ka jingiohpateng bad ka nongt^mmen jong u brieer kaba naduh mjnbarim eh ha ka jingsngew. jingtip, jingtbit, jittg* sngewthuh bad jingshemphang iaiakajong ka jinglong briew 'ha ka pyrthei bad ia ka jingiadei parabriew, ka jingiadei bad ka mat iang bad ka jingiadet bad u Blei.

Kane ka la kynthup lut ia ki jmgshem baroh jong ka jingim jinglong briew ha baroh ki bynta jong ka kat kumba la pynsah bad ai pateng ia ki ha kt jingthoh ha ki kot bad ki kitab kiba naduh mynbarim haduh mynta-mynne. II Hynrei, hadien ba ngi la iohi kattei ka don sa kawei pat ka jingmut jong kane ka ktien "Literature" kaba ngi lah ban ong ba ka long kaba kham bniah bad kaba kham pyrkhing. Ha kane ka Jingmut kane ka ktien ka kyntiuip tang ia kita ki jingthoh kiba iathuh ia ka jingshemjong uwei ne katto-katne ki bncw ha kano kano ka bynta Jong ka jingim jong ki lane baroh shi lynter jong ka lada ka long ha ka rukom iathuh>khana, ne ha ka rukom jingrwai ne ha ka rukom bi la buh kum ban thaw dur ia kata ka b^ynta jong kata ka jingshem ne Jingiakynduh jong ki ha ka dur jong ka Diama. Nalor kane ruh kane ka jingiathuh nejingpynpaw ka long kaba shai kdar kat ban da long ba kita kiba pule ne iobi ia ka jingiadei jong ka kumba ka da ja ne kumba ka da pynsngew ia kita shaphang jong kiba iathuh ne pyni ha ka jmgiathuhkhana, ka jingrwai, ne ka Drama, Ka jinglong kaba kongsan eh ha ka^ jingiathuh kumta bun ki 'riew pyrkhat bad ki nongthoh shaphang" kane ki ong, ba ka dei ban long ha ka rukom kaba don bor baa ktah la ka jingpyrkhat bad ia ka mynsicm jong ki shaphang ka jinglong-bnew bad ban ai jingkyntu ia ki ha ka jingiashah ne sngewlem bad ka jinglong briew, ne hikai ia ki da ka jingshem jong kiwei ban nang kham kyniiew ia la ka jinglong sha ka baa nang kham bha bad nang kham janai. Ill Ka "Literature" namar kata ka tasnoh bad ka jlngiitl ngi ki briew ha kane ka pyrthei. Ka pynpaw ia ka jiflgffh u briew ha ki jingiadei jong u baroh bad ia ki jingsh sha kiei baroh kiba sawdong jong u ha k a jingim ka met jingpyrkhat jong u bad ka mynsiem jong u, bad, kumba bynta kaba II haneog. ka buh dak ne pyrqmw ia kg jk||Ppy^, jingpynkhih ia ka mynsiem jong u da kine kiei kiei bareh dong jong II, sbiban kumba ka shob ha ka jingmut jong it iloiitliiitK Ka jingdawa kaba nyngkong eh jong u nongbishar oe nong* wadbniab sbaphang jong ka te ka paw shai ba ka long kaba del ban long kaba pynpaw ia kajingshisha lada ka long kaei kaei ruh, lada ka long shaphang u briew ne lada ka long sbaphang ka jinglong ka mariang. Ki drama u Shakespeare bad u Kalidasa, baba da niew kyrteng ia ki nongthoh drama kiba khrawtam tong ka pyrtbei, ki long kiba iai sab bad pjwnam haduh kane ka sngi namar ki long kiba shisha ha ka jingpynih jong ki ia ka dur ka jinglongbriew bad jingmut jingpyrkhat briew; ki pynpaw ia ka jingkhraw jingpyrkhat jong kitei ki nongthoh ha ka jingsngewthub jong ki ia ka jinglong kajingmut- briew (Psychology); bad katba ka jinglong briew kam pat kylla ha ki Jinglong tynrai jong ka kin iai long kiba iai thym* mai barabor, namar uno uno u briew ne ka br ew kiba pule ia ki km iaisngew ia ki jingsngew kiba ki nongthoh ki kwah ban kyrsiew ha ki da kaba kt^h ia ki jingshgew ba tynrai shaphang ka jingieit, ka jingsngewbha, ka jingsngewsih bad ka jingbitar. Ki briew baroh kin iasngewlem ia ka jinglui-lui jong ka Des>1emona; kin iaisngewsih ia ka jingkyrkieh jong u Othello ; kin iaisngcwsarong ha la ka jinglong briew kaba lah ban ktew sha ka jingdonbor bad jingbha kum ka jong u Othello ; kin iaisngewingkhong ia u lago bad ki buit shet-shalai jong u. Kumta. katba ka jingthewdor ia ka jingleh- jingkam bad ka jinglong briew ka dang sah kumjuh u Shakespeare un dang neh bad ki drama jong u kin dang iailong ki mawkordor jong ka Literature jong ka pyrthei. IV Ka don ka jingiapher'jingmut hapdeng katto-katne ki nongpyrkhat shaphang kane kawei ka hang ha ka jingbishar ia ka Literature ^ kata shaphang kaba pynpaw ia ka jingim jong u briew ha ka pyrthei. Kiba bud ia kawei ka rukom pyrkhat ki ong ba ka dei ban long kum ka !t-khmih kaba pynpaw janai ia ka jmgim ba ki Hang jong ka baroh bad ia baroh kijmgjia kiba shisha ha ka Kumba ngi tip baroh ki don ki jingshisha kiba ihtriem, kiba pyrshah ia ka jingmutdur jong ngi ia kiei'kiei kiba itynnad bad ba shongkhia ha ka jmgim. Kum ia kine baroh, kita ki nongpyrkhat ki ong, dei ban pynpaw shai ia ki ba ka literatuie, kum ban ong noh, ha ka jinglyngkhuid jong ki baroh khiem da da shuh na ka byota ka jingdonakor. namar ki ong, ki long ki jingshisha jong ka jingim.

Kine ki ong ba ki pUd ba ngi buh ia ka jinglongdonburom bad jinglongdonakor ki long kiba ngi shu thaw hi ma ngi ki briew bad n mar<kata kirn don bynta satia ha ka literature kaba long ka itkhmih ha kaba ka jingim ka shat bad ka paw ne phalang pat. Kiwei pat Id don kiba pyrkhat tnt kam tong satia ka kam Jong Lit^fdturc ban tbftd Ir* ilnoim kriAu/ pamat ba kata kan ym ii^nnad ia ka jinjm ka< kiha donakor, ba ka iingim ka bynii pyrshang bail ia kytuoh ka lohg ka jingim ka bym shym khaoi halor ia ka jmgira jotig Id mrad bad ka long pynban kajingim kaba iap. Kane ka jingmui kumne shaphang ka Literature ka kdew beit sha kawei pat jinglongjong ka kaba long, ki dawa, kawei pat ka bynta kaba kongsan jong ka kam jong ka. Kata ka long, ba ka kam jong ka^ Literature ka long ban pynpaw, hooid, la kajingim, hynrei pat ban shim jingring jingmut na kiei-kiei kiba ngi iohih ba kin long ka, jingiarap ba ngin bishar hok ia u briew ha ka jingloiig^briew jong u, kum uba mihkhmat na ka iaid ba long-briew baroh ha kyllci^, ka pyrthei bad ba da kaba leh kumta ban lah ruh^ban nang pyni* i tynnad bad nangpynjanai ia ka. My subject to-night is the Rudiments of the Khasi Law of Inheritance, At the outset I must tell you that this law of inheritance amongst the Khasis fall under the general classifi* cation of ‘ The Customs’’ or “Customary Law”. It is need- less for me to tell you what a custom is, but, in jurisprudence, in order to be valid it has to satisfy some requirements. The Judicial Committee has explained it as follows: “Custom i» a rule which in a particular family or in a particular district has from long usages obtained the force of law. It must be ancient, certain and reasonable and being in derogation of the general rule of law, must be construed strictly. ’ Antiquity, certainty, reasonableness and continuity are essential to the va- lidity of a custom. Most of the Khasi customs will be found to satisfy these requirements and I do not think I should go inio this question at all.

Now a Khasi is a Khasi because of his religion (Niam) more than anything else. This is a great fact. To understand him therefore one has got to go deep down into the very root of his religion. It is ^religion in the sense of hia "Niam”, which regulates all his thoughts and actiWlies Forget his religion and you will never understand a Khasi. I believe that in no other department of his law does religion play sO prominent a part as in this law of inheritance. I propose to raise some questions and try to answer them as I believe this will help us a great deal to grasp this great fundamental fact enunciated above. My first question is how is it that in the case of all ancestral property, the Khadduto is the custodian ? Here I must strike a note of warning Some people think, especially foreigners, that the Khaddiib or last daughter succeeds to the property of the family : this is wrv wrong idea. She succeeds not to the property but to the as custodian or keeper of it. A question arises here and that is why women and not men are holders ot properties ? Tho answer is, I believe, because like David of old, their han^ were full of blood - constant warfare and bloodshed - they th^ght it best to leave the religion in the hands of their wotnen folk. Bradley Birt, Chapter vi). ««• ««* ««« Khasj Rehgion Rltea and RELIGION. In Khasi the word NIAM means the ceremonies rites and ceremonies. In the completion of these rites and ceremonies we have the duties to per- form as the bond of human family and society. Thus we have the marriage and birth ceremonies, the naming ceremonies, the death and the bone keeping ceremonies. These are the emotional and the practical aspects of Khasi religion • NIAM - as interpre- ted in act and behaviour and as embodied in custom and as forming family ties and social bonds. In these ceremonies we have the manifestation of the Khasi mind in words, deeds, cus- toms and institutions, and of their idea of the ultimate cause. Ultimate Cause In their idea of the ultimate cause we have the cognitive aspect which gives us the idea of their belief and of their position in which they place themselves with reference to this ultimate cause. It is their human yearning for knowledge and their struggling for freedom and the means to escape. How and whence difficult to say how and whence the this idea Khasis came to the idea of the ultimate cause to which they gave the name U Blei- GOD. It may be surmised that by synthetic and analytic me- thods Khasis realised that there is a higher unity which explains life and matter. They cannot explain how iife ceased, the only possible answer to the questions must have been the existence of a hi|iher unity which explains them all. These are the indi- cations in the Khasi phrases that they understood and realised life.

The phrase "ka long", ka man’. Ka long - to be, ka man - to grow. The tree lives - u dieng u long, and the potato (lubars) has grown - u phan ii la man. Then we find these words with references to themselves and the ultimate cause. "Ka long briew, ka man briew,” lit. - to be human and to grow human. Hence in the marriage ceremony the officiating priest says "Hei ko Blei na jrong na tbian, ko Lei synshar, ko Lej thaw briew man br'ew kumba la buh ma phi u Blei - ka Blei ban long f kha ban long I Man." “He! Oh God from above and below (that is of the heavens and earth) Oh God the controller. Oh God the Creator of the being of man and the growth of man, as ordained by thee U Biei - Ka Blei to be those who cause to be and who cause to grow, I Kha - 1 Man” (lit. those who are connected by marriage). ^°tran8ci^ncv There is the Khasi conception of the transciency and vanity and vanity of the world of experience and he called this state of imperfection "ka pyrthei shong basa” (lit. the world of temporary abode or residence) and with reference to his material existence he says "ka ruh shong bynda" (Ht the life of temporary encasement) which show his- idea of temporal world and temporal existence. • 75 — , na.«« of saw life never ceased, there is the’cycfeV SSs"“h'i.‘^e seeds germinates springs, grows and ripens, so bS saT ‘loiS and man ‘to be and ‘to grow’. Thus in their reSStion of as^'iTIfinlte ®and ilf*exDerieSli"*^?*lf Indestructible. experience of life as transcient and vain, .

cycle ot life, Khasis bad attained to the cognitive aspect of their belief in a creator who is supe- rior to temporariness and finitude, that is in a God who is trancendent and immanent. In iheir realisation of the cycle of life they also realised that life as well as the ultimate is indes- tructible. Order and economy. In this cycle of life they also realised that there is order and economy; they attributed all this to the cha- racter of the ultimate cause. Attributes of Having stated all these you will see in the Kha- "U Blei" God. si expressions of the attributes of this ultimate cause whom they caU*’‘U Blei” God, which will explain and bear out in all that I have said : — U Blei Nongthaw Nongbuh - God the creator of our bodies and the creation (Nongthaw), and God who fills us and fills the universe with life - Nongbuh mynsiem. U Blei Trai Kynrad - The Lord God and master. V Blei shi hajarnguh- God to whom all obeisance is due. U Blei na jrong na thian - God who fills the heavens and the earth (the universe.) God who is immanent and transcendent. V Blei U Nongsei - God who causes to be and to grow. U Blei uba iohi uba tip - God who sees and who know • to whom nothing is hidden or unknown. Let me quote some of the instances in which these attributes appear. We find in the birth ceremony the sacrificer implores, “Ko Blei ko Nongthaw ko Nongbah" “Oh God the creator and God the instiller of life”. The other attributes are used in the dtffertmt ceremonies adapting to the occasions and ceremonies performed, but all these attributes appear in the ceremony of thaQks giving offering to God. when the sacrficer siys “sngew ko Biei Trai Kynrad, na Jrong na tbian, ko nongthaw ko nongbuh, kj> nongfhu'ng, ko nongsei, kumba ngh la long bynfiew, man “Hear Oh God Lord and master of the heavens and the ear® ifflh 76 - (universe), the creator and the instiller, the appointer, who causest to grow who causest to be, as I have become mankind, grown and increased in mankind.” These ceremonies with the Khasi epithets applied to Him whom they call U Blei, God, show the Khasi theistic idea of the oneness of that God to whom all obeisance is due (shi hajar nguh).

In this monotheistic idea of God there is a notion of the feminine attribute in the God'head in whom the control and care of Hie in the universe is entrusted. God th® Controller This attribute is personified as Ka Lei Ke Lei Synshar Synshar (God the Law giver and controller). This attribute of God plays a very important part in the Khasi conception of God and of the system of the divine dispensation and the economy in the world. The Khasi believes and has a clear conception of God as the law giver to the human race which in the Khasi legend is known as the “HynBiew trep hynniew skum” — “the seven nests the seven roots”. He is the God the creator and God who fills the heavens and th<* earth (najrong na tbian) and to whom all obeisance should be paid (shi hajar nguh). Sickness and A Khasi attributes to his acts of transgression Calamities against God and his sins of omission and commission, the cause cf sickness and calamities in whieh the evil spirits and forces of nature take an active part. Thus the Khasi practices divination to find out the cause and propitiate these spirits and forces. But these forces are under the control of God, and the Khasi as a last resoit when everything else fails, leaves it to the will of God. The Khasi is also aware of sin against God and the order of God It is a “sang”, (Sah-ang— that which remains gaping, that which cannot be reconciled), that which cannot be filled up-hence cannot be reconciled before the justice of God. M in ,A,hnm Again we find the Khasi says, “Ap fhe^ power to revSard jutfng me U Blei, ieng rangbah Me and to punish is vested u briew” (Hold up the covenant thou. Oh God, arise and«6upport, oh man). When he is baffled by the evil device of his fellow man he leaves everything to God, and last of all to the day when both he and the other man will take their stand before and bo judged by Him, Veneration of Khasis adore deceased an« •ncestor cestors by means of offerings. These ancestors are U Saidnia (the first ma« teroal uncle), ka lawbei (the first grand*inothef) and u Thawlanjg (the first father, husbhnd of ka lawbei), I shall return to thus again later. - 77 - A chatlAnge This veneration of ancestors and the attempt to secure material prosperity by revering spedal objects, throws out a challenge as to whether the idea of rdi* gion in the world degenerated from the idea of God to idolatry and fetichism, or was a progressive idea from the latter to God and the submission of man to God.

Relation betwer. The Khasi belief in the prayer asking for man ar.d God forgiveness of God the Creator, Lora ana Master, of his sins and acts of transgres- gression after he had been able to ascertain them by divinations^ tends more to prove that a Khasi allows nothing of material gain to stand between him and God, and that all other things, the sacrifices for ancestors and the offerings for objects of spe-* cial favour, are motives proceeding from selfish and lower ideas of life, and therefore indicate a degeneration of man from the aspiration for higher to the passion for the lower ends of human life,. Thus I have already said, in the Khasi ceremonies, oflfe- rings and sacrifices we find that God the Creator Himself is invoked in tbis way : ‘‘Sngew ko Blei Trai Kyorad na jrong na tbian, ko Nongthaw, ko Nongbuh, ko Nongthung, ko Nongj sci, kumba nga ia long bynriew, man bynriew la ioh ka khiah ka nang, kumba la isynei ma phi ka Blei ka trai kynrad “Give ear, oh God Lord and master of above and below, thou who Cfeatest, thou who placest, thou who plantest, thou who causest to grow, as I have been made human, have received health through thy mercies, God, Lord and master, and so on. There is no space in this paper, to describe the different sacrifices and offerings and ceremonies and means of divination^ but it will suffice to say that God in the male attributes of Creator, Lord and Master— U Xeithaw, and God in the female attributes of Keeper, Controller and Preserver,— Ka Blei Synshaf^ is the God to whom the Khasi pays his homage and performs acs of obeisance by offerings and ceremonies. Others are only means of propitiation to ward off evil influences or to tiate evil Influences and spirits who cannot have P^^er ov^ men except God the Keeper (Ka Blet) gives them to punish man for his sins and acts of omission and (ka tyrut ka smer, ka lait ka let, tod ka^ sang). The MW ceremonies consist in "Ka kheiS ka bi^ar, K*®® on khrei”, and ka “Tap rwiang ka ksan mgiew. In M khein ka bishar" man for h s hfe and thanks. to God. In "kaon ksuid toon the evil spirits and influences. In ^ rogiew'* man Mcriaces to regain or ^otect to, Ttos word "ragieW* mews man s S«*«l hate (jiurs) which gives personality wd snucHty* - 78 - Cows, goats, pigs, fowls and hen's eggs are used in cereme* tales. Pigeons are also used in the "On ksuid on khrei" cere- fnoniss. The cock has a unique and important significance in the Khasi divination, so also the divination by hen's eggs. Divination by egg breaking is a special f ature in the Khasi religious rites It is performed on a specially made wooden board and the egg besmeared with red earth the sacrihcer addresses: '"Ko leng sam khun Ka Blei ko ba nang ko ba tip," Oh Leng> sam (Leng is a concentration for the woi d ‘Pylleng’ eggs), thou child of God (ka blei) thou who hast been acquainted or art aware and thou who knowest." The egg is then dashed on the board and the position of the fragments of egg shell are read as either good or evil prognostics according to certain rules by which the positions of egg fragments are interpreted. Animistic ideas There are in Khasi practices what are inclu- ded tn the present day defination of animism, but from what I have described of the Khasi idea and the Khasis is not a creation of animism. He is not a ‘magnified non-na- tural man*, he is not seen.

Wsa Of*life^ft€^ Bone keeping ceremonies. The veneration of death ancestors provides a strong social bond The successive ceremonies performed from the moment the body has been cremated, when the bones are collected from the funeral pyre, to the time these bones are taken and interred in their last resting place of the mawniam, the stone cist where all the the successive ceremonies performed at varying times after death, are terminated, with the creation of memorial stones, fjfdicate the idea in which he p*aces himself behind the dead and the living. The ceremonies are so laid down and continued fii'om time to time by tlie living as not to forget their dead. Thus in the idea of their connection with dead Khasis keep alive their connection with the living, the ‘kur* (blood relations) and the ‘Kha* those related by marriage not only through their own but also of their deceased relatives, that is the children of their deceased relatives, and of their duty towards them, tiiat is to the world around th«n. For this the Khasis fear tihe Sang. Further the ceremonies are a testimony to their belief fhal their dead livje after this life, and that life is a continua- tSto of this life in the sense that the life beyond does not fbi^get of its mst and of its connection with life on this side 6f the funeral pyre. Hence the sacrificer at the food offerings addressed the dead, saying, "Hei tale (naming the dead personally br eoltdctively 'ff more tfikn one) wat buh khoh wat bub jaw," tlmt Is (thdu so and so), Have no regrets, have no bitte r.ess, tyiij^t me u Ni. me tt Kong, sneng ryngkat me u tongkha me % man kha/' Thbn <u 41), dboa -79— brother (U kong) favour him (i.e. the dead) with your counsel, thou who causest to be (U long kha) thou who causest to grow (U man 'kha) give kindly counsel (meaning to the dead). Ha ing u Biel. Lastly. 1 cannot say how and when the cere« (Hcu«© of God.) monies are initiated, but the laborious ceremo- nies performed at varying times, and in successive forms in tho bone keeping ceremonies indicate a culture which has withstood the batterings of time, and it is also true that in spite of these ceremonies the Khasi theistic ideas have not been bequiled by the shadowy objects, and ceremonies. To the Khasi, He is the Ood to whom the Khasi resigns himself in prayer and to whom he pays his obeisance, and the Crod to w'hom he hopes to go ‘Ha ing u Blei’ there in the house of God after Icadim; a life of “Tip hok tip sot’, a life of righteousness and truthfulness. — David Roy

My subject to-night is the Rudiments of the Khasi Law of Inheritance, At the outset I must tell you that this law of inheritance amongst the Khasis fall under the general classifi* cation of ‘ The Customs’’ or “Customary Law”. It is need- less for me to tell you what a custom is, but, in jurisprudence, in order to be valid it has to satisfy some requirements. The Judicial Committee has explained it as follows: “Custom i» a rule which in a particular family or in a particular district has from long usages obtained the force of law. It must be ancient, certain and reasonable and being in derogation of the general rule of law, must be construed strictly. ’ Antiquity, certainty, reasonableness and continuity are essential to the va- lidity of a custom. Most of the Khasi customs will be found to satisfy these requirements and I do not think I should go inio this question at all.

Now a Khasi is a Khasi because of his religion (Niam) more than anything else. This is a great fact. To understand him therefore one has got to go deep down into the very root of his religion. It is ^religion in the sense of hia "Niam”, which regulates all his thoughts and actiWlies Forget his religion and you will never understand a Khasi. I believe that in no other department of his law does religion play sO prominent a part as in this law of inheritance. I propose to raise some questions and try to answer them as I believe this will help us a great deal to grasp this great fundamental fact enunciated above. My first question is how is it that in the case of all ancestral property, the Khadduto is the custodian ? She succeeds not to the property but to the as custodian or keeper of it. A question arises here and that is why women and not men are holders ot properties ?
